citation: corpus/herdr-0.8.0/api-schema.json, which herdr generates from its own request types and ./dev checks the running daemon against. Method names and every parameter here are declared there: PaneSplitParams (cwd, direction, env, focus, ratio, target_pane_id, workspace_id), TabCreateParams (cwd, env, focus, label, workspace_id), WorkspaceCreateParams (cwd, env, focus, label), LayoutSetSplitRatioParams (pane_id, path, ratio, tab_id), PaneResizeParams (amount, direction, pane_id), PaneZoomParams (mode, pane_id) whose mode defaults to toggle. The direction pair is recorded in docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md.
why: herdr ignores a parameter it does not recognise rather than refusing the request (`observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` section 6), so a misspelled key does not fail - it acts on whatever the daemon happened to have focused. `pane.split` is the sharp one: it takes `target_pane_id` where every other pane verb takes `pane_id`, and sending the wrong one splits an arbitrary pane. Against a real daemon holding one workspace and one pane, that is indistinguishable from correct, which is why these are pinned by name here rather than left to the daemon-backed tests. The second half is the direction pair: Muster names a split for the arrangement it produces and herdr for where the new pane goes, and `layout.rs` reads that same pair back in reverse - so getting it wrong here makes a column that reads back as a row.

cases.name: a split names the pane to split, in the key only pane.split uses
cases.why: The silent one. `pane_id` here is dropped without complaint and herdr splits whichever pane it has focused, which in a window with one pane looks exactly right. Also the absent half of the envelope: no ratio and no directory are asked for, because sending nulls would be Muster stating a preference it does not have. herdr's own default ratio is what a keybinding wants, and its default directory is the one the split came from - which is what somebody splitting a pane mid-task means.

cases.name: a row is a split downwards
cases.why: Muster names a split for the arrangement it makes and herdr for where the pane went. layout.rs reads the same pair backwards, so a wrong mapping here produces a tree that disagrees with itself.

cases.name: a dragged-out split states both
cases.why: The other half of the same rule: a drag has an opinion about the ratio, and a pane opened for a directory has one about where it starts.

cases.name: a tab names the workspace it goes in, because nothing else can
cases.why: tab.create takes a workspace and nothing else - there is no pane_id it would accept - so the workspace is resolved from the mirror before the intent is built. A hopeful pane_id would be ignored and the tab would land wherever that daemon was focused.

cases.name: a tab with nowhere named falls back to the daemon's own rule
cases.why: Reachable when the pane the keyboard is on has no directory yet. A home directory is a worse answer than the one somebody wanted, and a better one than refusing to make the tab.

cases.name: a workspace names nothing, and lets herdr label it
cases.why: The intent asked for when there is nothing: a daemon Muster just started holds no panes. A label invented here would be a second naming scheme for something herdr already names, and the null is explicit because the key exists and Muster is declining it.

cases.name: closing and focusing a pane use the ordinary key
cases.why: The counterweight to the split case: `pane_id` is right everywhere except pane.split, so a reader who learns target_pane_id from that one case would spread it.

cases.name: focus names the pane the daemon should call looked-at
cases.why: Written rather than read: Muster routes input by its own cursor and tells the daemon so that whatever it computes from focus has been told (architecture.md, cursors are written, not read).

cases.name: a dragged divider is addressed by the turns down to it
cases.why: Dividers have no ids - a divider is a position in a shape that changes under it - so the path is how herdr names one. First is false and second is true, which is the same spelling layout.rs reads trees back with.

cases.name: the root divider is an empty path, not a missing one
cases.why: Dragging the only divider in a tab takes no turns to reach. An omitted path is a different request - herdr requires one - so this pins that zero turns is spelled as an empty array.

cases.name: resizing names a pane and a direction, and no divider
cases.why: The difference from layout.set_split_ratio, which is the other way to move the same line. A chord means `this pane bigger`; which divider achieves that is a question about a tree the person pressing it is not looking at, and only the daemon holds the rectangles that answer it.

cases.name: an amount is sent only when somebody meant one
cases.why: A keybinding wants the daemon's own step, and stating a number here would be Muster inventing a step size it has no opinion about. A CLI or an agent placing a divider exactly says.

cases.name: zoom asks for a toggle by not asking for anything
cases.why: herdr's own default for `mode` is toggle, which is what one key means. Sending it would be Muster restating a default it agrees with - and the day that default changes is the day this should notice rather than quietly keep the old behaviour.
